Minister
min'is-ter
n. and v. (a servant; to serve; rendering Hebrew sharath, Greek diakoneo and diakonos)
From Latin minister, a servant or attendant, built on minus, less — the opposite of magister, a master, built on magis, more. The word means an underling, and every ecclesiastical dignity attached to it since has been at war with its etymology.

Biblical Definition

Minister means a servant, and it is used in Scripture of three distinct services. It is used of a personal attendant: “Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua” (Exodus 24:13), and of the synagogue attendant who took the scroll back from Christ at Nazareth (Luke 4:20) — a functionary handling a book, in the most consequential reading in history. It is used of sacred service: the Levite “shall minister in the name of the LORD his God” (Deuteronomy 18:7), and Hezekiah charges the priests that the LORD has chosen them “to stand before him, to serve him, and that ye should minister unto him” (2 Chronicles 29:11). And strikingly, Paul applies the word to the civil magistrate, twice in one verse: “he is the minister of God to thee for good... for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Romans 13:4). The word is also used of what ordinary speech can do: talk that is good to the use of edifying “may minister grace unto the hearers” (Ephesians 4:29).

Webster 1828 Definition

A servant or attendant, and the verb to serve. In Scripture it covers the personal attendant, the Levite in sacred service, the civil magistrate as God's minister for good, and the speech that ministers grace to those who hear it.

expand to see more

MINISTER, n. [L. minister, from minus, less; opposed to magister, from magis, more.] A servant; one who attends and serves another.

2. One to whom a sovereign or a state entrusts the direction of affairs; a magistrate.

3. One who serves at the altar; one charged with the cure of souls; a pastor.

4. MINISTER, v.i. To attend and serve; to supply things needful; as, to minister to the sick.

5. In Scripture, his minister Joshua, Exo. 24; he is the minister of God to thee for good, Rom. 13.

Key Scripture

Exodus 24:13 — "And Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua: and Moses went up into the mount of God."

Deuteronomy 18:7 — "Then he shall minister in the name of the LORD his God, as all his brethren the Levites do, which stand there before the LORD."

Romans 13:4 — "For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil."

Ephesians 4:29 — "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."

Modern Corruption

A word that means underling has been made a title of rank. Christ founded the office on service and set Himself as the pattern, and every clerical system that reverses this — whether by vestment, by hierarchy, or by celebrity — has inverted the word it uses.

expand to see more

The Lord's teaching is explicit and is given precisely because the disciples were disputing about rank: ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them... but it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister. He then grounds it in His own coming — not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give His life a ransom for many. The Roman hierarchy, with its graded orders culminating in a papal monarchy, is the most developed contradiction of this, and the Reformation named it as such; but Protestant celebrity is the same sin in modern dress, and its practitioners are usually the last to see it.

The remedy is not a false humility about the office, which is genuinely honourable. Scripture says the elder who rules well is worthy of double honour, and requires that the congregation esteem such men very highly in love for their work's sake. What it does not permit is dominion — Peter, who might have claimed it, charges elders to feed the flock not as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. Two offices, elder and deacon; a plurality of elders; and a word for both that means servant.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sharath is to minister or attend, used of Joshua under Moses and of the Levites before the LORD; Greek diakoneo is to serve, especially at table, and diakonos gives both the general word for minister and the office of deacon.

expand to see more

Hebrew sharath (H8334) — to minister, attend, serve; used of both personal and sacred service.

Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve, especially to wait at table; the verb Christ applies to Himself.

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant or attendant; the word for the minister and for the office of deacon.

Greek leitourgos (G3011) — a public servant; used of the magistrate and of ministers of the sanctuary.

Latin minister — from minus, less; an underling, the opposite of magister, a master.

Usage

"Of a personal attendant to a prophet: Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua (Exodus 24:13)."

"Of the civil magistrate as God's servant: he is the minister of God to thee for good (Romans 13:4)."

"Of speech that serves those who hear it: that it may minister grace unto the hearers (Ephesians 4:29)."
